To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the returns to education are higher in the private than in the public sector, (2) the returns to experience are higher in the public than in the private sector, (3) the returns to schooling are higher than the returns to experience, (4) the returns to both schooling and experience are higher than the return to sex, and (5) the returns to all three factors are higher than the average rate of return in other developing countries.

the private sector is more responsive than the public sector in rewarding education; that the public sector puts a premium on work experience; and that the general returns to schooling in Indonesia are very high.

(1) the private sector pays more than the public sector for each additional year or level of schooling and for each year of experience; (2) the public sector pays more than private sector for experience but less for schooling; (3) the sex differential disappears once experience is allowed to vary with education; (4) the rate of return to schooling is 15-17% in Indonesia, which is very high by international standards.

the analysis of the returns to education, experience and sex in the public and private sectors of urban Java.
the effect of schooling, work experience and sex on earnings in the urban labour market of Indonesia.

the private sector is more efficient than the public sector in using education as an input in the production of income, but the public sector is better at using experience.

the returns to education in urban Indonesia are high, and the private sector plays a key role in this regard.
